title: QH 207 / Qubbet el-Hawa — Osiris repair-casting, gilded old bronze, ritual deposition and Elephantine context source audit
method: Source-bound extraction from Fitzenreiter, Willer and Auenmüller 2016. Analytical/archival observations are separated from author interpretation and from JANUS hypotheses. No literal relic identity is promoted from ritual or mythological parallels.

source.work: Martin Fitzenreiter, Frank Willer and Johannes Auenmüller, Materialien einer Gusswerkstatt von der Qubbet el-Hawa, Bonner Aegyptiaca, Berlin: EB-Verlag, 2016
source.google_drive_path: /Google Drive/JANUS Research/QH207 Qubbet el-Hawa/Materialien einer Gusswerkstatt von der Qubbet el-Hawa (Fitzenreiter-Willer-Auenmueller 2016).pdf
source_classes: original excavation/fundbook quotations reproduced in publication

QH_207_32.description: Osiris statuette with bronze foot; wax + bronze
QH_207_32.relation_to_38: The bronze foot is highly probably the missing fourth Osiris figure associated with QH 207/38; archive/radiograph-card documentation explicitly directs comparison with QH 207/32.

QH_207_38.description: casting mould for four Osiris statuettes
QH_207_38.technical_observation: Four wax Osiris figures were modelled directly onto existing bronze foot fragments; technologically grouped with QH 207/39 and /40 as reconstruction/overcasting forms.

QH_207_39.technical_observation: Three bronze foot/lower-body fragments were completed in wax. A fourth inverted Osiris was a previously hollow-cast composite broken in several parts; its loose head was fixed with an approximately 2 cm quadrangular metal pin, possibly iron. The foot may not belong to the same original figure.
QH_207_39.important_negative_control: At least one foot fragment preserves an extra feed channel indicating a workshop-fresh failed casting that had not yet been mounted on a base; therefore not every fragment in the special group can be classified as a previously used cult object.

QH_207_40.analytical_receipt: A very thin gold layer on one Osiris foot/lower fragment was detected by HDR microscopy and verified at LVR-LandesMuseum Bonn with a Niton XL3t portable XRF instrument. Because leaf gilding is applied after casting and surface finishing, this fragment necessarily belonged to an already finished cast before reuse in the repair form.

QH_207_55.technical_observation: Fragment of the same special repair group. A hollow-cast bronze Osiris foot/lower fragment was substantially remodelled in wax in preparation for an overcast/reconstruction casting. The mould remained unburnt and the final repair cast was not completed.

technical_synthesis.reason: The special group contains both evidence for a previously finished/gilded object and evidence for at least one workshop-fresh failed cast. The lifecycle must therefore remain mixed rather than generalized.

receipts: Contemporary excavation diary entries refer to 'small finds from the pot' and 'finds from the jug' in the Burial 1 sequence and support association of the technological assemblage with this context.

Jürgen Wentscher later recalled QH 207/42, /43 and /132 in a slender vessel at the foot end of Coffin 1, but later recollection and reconstructed provenance do not fully eliminate ambiguity for every individual item.
The publication explicitly notes that the excavation documentation does not differentiate every small find object-by-object within the vessel context.
Burial 1 is probably associated, through the Ptah-Sokar-Osiris statuette, with Rer, a sistrum-player of Satet of Elephantine.
Male owners among the Late Period burials are identified by titles as priests of Khnum / the Elephantine triad; women are temple musicians.
The publication describes the deceased as socially and geographically connected with the priestly elite of Elephantine.
elephantine_context.boundary: This social/geographic context does not by itself establish a local First Cataract physical-relic tradition for the repaired statuettes.

published_interpretation_receipts: The authors argue that the exceptional effort of repair is difficult to explain on purely technical grounds because remelting and recasting would have been easier; they discuss preservation of divine figures as a motivating factor.
The interpretive chapter considers funerary offering, workshop remains and sacred depot, and ultimately gives strong weight to ritual deposition of sacralized transformative material.
The publication explicitly discusses the completion of 'zerstückelten' Osiris figures as potentially reflecting aspects of the Osiris myth and funerary transformation.
It also considers the possibility that wax completion and embedding in mould material constituted a magically effective 'healing' state even without the final bronze overcast.
The same chapter states that broader Osiris-myth/transformation concepts are more important than the comparatively secondary relation to local sacred entities.

open_questions_for_authors.question: Where are QH 207/32 and QH 207/38 now, and do transfer records, additional negatives, radiograph cards or photographs survive that could test the physical association more directly?

Do the full muCT volumes/segmentations for QH 207/39, /40 and /55 still survive and can they be made available for scholarly inspection? Has any later non-destructive work tested additional fragments for gilding or other surface finishing since 2016?

After later work, including publications after 2016, is a specifically local First Cataract/Elephantine Osirian relic tradition considered supportable for this assemblage, or should the interpretation remain at the broader Osiris myth / dismemberment / transformation level?

Frank_Foerster.next: No duplicate request; he advised contacting the authors for remaining interpretive questions.
